records.title: Light, loose cotton clothing
records.category_basis: Described as a long-standing practice in Rajasthan by the Churu plan and reported as a current adaptation by workers in Bangladesh; also general public health advice.

local_names.name: angarkha
local_names.note: a loose upper garment, named in the Churu plan

records.summary: Wearing light-coloured, loose, breathable cotton clothes in the hot season, described in Rajasthan's Churu plan and reported by construction workers in Bangladesh. WHO and UNICEF give the same general advice.
records.description: The Churu plan describes loose, breathable cotton garments in light shades as a traditional way of dressing for heat in Rajasthan. In a survey of construction and welding workers in Bangladesh, wearing loose clothing was among the adaptive behaviours workers reported.
records.mechanism: Loose, breathable fabric lets air move over the skin and sweat evaporate; light colours reflect more sunlight. This is the general basis of the official advice; no study here measured it for these garments.
records.benefits: Low cost where clothes are already owned; consistent with WHO and UNICEF advice.
records.uncertain: How much it lowers heat strain for a given garment, work or humidity has not been measured in these sources.
records.fails_when: Work clothing, uniforms or protective equipment are required; in very humid heat evaporation slows; dress norms may limit choice.
records.contraindications: Not a substitute for rest, shade, water and cooler spaces in dangerous heat.
records.labour: Washing and drying more often in the hot season
records.equity: Workers who must wear employer-issued uniforms or protective gear may not be able to choose; women's dress norms may differ by place.

who.decides: The wearer, or the employer for uniforms

evaluation: Does a given garment change skin temperature, sweat rate or heat strain during real work?
Do uniform rules allow lighter clothing in the hot season?

records.title: Rajasthani garments and head coverings (as described in the Churu plan)
records.category_basis: Named garments described by the Churu plan as traditional; the plan does not cite a study of them.

local_names.name: lehariya turban
local_names.note: a tie-dyed turban, named for men

local_names.name: odhni
local_names.note: a head and shoulder covering, named for women

local_names.name: lehenga
local_names.note: a long skirt, named for women

records.summary: The Churu plan names turbans, odhnis, angarkhas and lehengas as garments that allow airflow while shielding from the sun, and says layered clothing protects by insulating against hot air. These are the plan's descriptions; no measurement is cited.
records.description: The plan lists angarkha and lehariya turbans for men and odhnis and lehengas for women. It states that layered clothing, "paradoxically", protects against heat by minimising direct exposure.
records.mechanism: Covering the head and skin reduces direct sun on the body; the claim that layers insulate against hot air is the plan's, and may hold only in very dry heat with strong sun. Not tested in these sources.
records.benefits: Culturally familiar; covers the head from direct sun.
records.uncertain: Whether layering helps or harms depends on humidity, air speed and work rate; untested here.
records.fails_when: Humid heat or heavy work, where layers trap sweat; garments that restrict movement at work.
records.contraindications: Not a substitute for shade, rest and water.
records.equity: Dress norms differ by gender, caste and community; the plan presents men's and women's garments separately.
evaluation: Measure head and skin temperature with and without these coverings in dry and in humid heat.
Ask wearers when coverings help and when they make heat worse.

records.title: Mud, hay and thatch houses, with more openings
records.category_basis: Older residents describe earlier kutcha houses built from local materials; the study does not identify them as Indigenous.

local_names.name: kutcha house
local_names.note: a house with roofs and walls of mud, bamboo, clay, cow dung or other natural materials, as the study defines it

records.summary: Older villagers in Jodhpur district recalled that houses with mud-and-hay walls and roofs, or thatched roofs, stayed cooler than tin-sheet and closed concrete houses, and described adding windows for ventilation.
records.description: Participants described thatched roofs that deflect direct sun, mud and hay walls and roofs, and additional windows. Some contrasted these with newer tin-sheet roofs that "get hot quickly" and closed concrete houses.
records.mechanism: Thatch and earth can limit heat passing through the roof and release it more slowly than thin metal sheets; openings let air move. Plausible, but not measured in this study.
records.benefits: Uses local materials; residents describe them as cooler than tin roofs.
records.uncertain: No temperatures were measured; how these houses compare at night, in humid spells or with today's longer heatwaves is unknown.
records.fails_when: Thatch needs regular renewal; earth walls need protection from rain; materials or skills may no longer be available; fire risk with thatch.
records.contraindications: Safety, fire and structural checks before any retrofit; not a reason to avoid durable safe housing.
records.labour: Building and seasonal repair, often family labour
records.equity: Many households have moved to tin and concrete for durability, status or housing schemes; returning to earthen roofs is a choice only some can make.
evaluation: Measure indoor air temperature in earthen, tin and concrete homes on the same days, including nights.
What maintenance and fire-safety support would households need?

records.title: Lime or alum coating of roofs and floors, and lime plaster
records.category_basis: Reported by villagers in Jodhpur district and described in older Bikaner buildings and the Churu plan.
records.summary: Villagers in Jodhpur district described coating roofs and floors with limestone or alum to keep houses cool; lime plaster is part of older buildings in Bikaner and is encouraged in the Churu plan. Its separate effect on indoor temperature has not been measured in these sources.
records.description: Participants said a house with a thatched roof, open windows and a roof coated with limestone or alum "remains cool". A study of Bikaner describes lime plaster inside red brick walls of older buildings, but does not report measurements that isolate its effect.
records.mechanism: A pale lime surface reflects more sunlight than a dark one; lime plaster also takes up and releases moisture. Whether either lowers indoor temperature here is untested.
records.benefits: Low-cost, familiar materials.
records.uncertain: Effect on indoor air temperature is not measured; the Bikaner study treats thermal mass and insulation as one property, which they are not.
records.fails_when: Coatings wear off and need renewing; alum and lime handling needs care.
records.contraindications: Lime is caustic when fresh: skin and eye protection while mixing and applying.
records.equity: Renters may not be allowed to alter roofs.
evaluation: Measure roof surface and room air temperature before and after coating, against an uncoated roof.
How often does a coating need renewing?

records.title: Wet sacks or cloths over doors and windows
records.category_basis: Reported by villagers as a current household practice.
records.summary: Some villagers in Jodhpur district hang wet sacks or cloths over doors and windows to keep hot air out. It relies on evaporation, which works best in dry air and needs water.
records.description: Respondents described hanging wet sacks or cloths over doors and windows to prevent hot air from entering the house.
records.mechanism: Air passing through a wet cloth is cooled by evaporation, as in an evaporative cooler. This works best when the air is dry; it adds humidity indoors. Not measured in this study.
records.benefits: Uses materials at hand.
records.uncertain: How much it cools a room, and for how long, is unmeasured.
records.fails_when: Humid weather (little evaporation, more indoor humidity); water shortage, which the same villages report; damp can encourage mould.
records.contraindications: Not useful in humid heat; keep rooms ventilated.
records.labour: Re-wetting through the day, often by women at home
records.equity: Depends on water that households in these villages buy from tankers in summer.
evaluation: Measure room temperature and humidity with and without wet screens on dry and humid days.

records.title: Cooking early and late, and stoves outside
records.category_basis: Reported household practice.
records.summary: Households in Jodhpur district cook very early and late in the day, store food for the afternoon, and place stoves in setbacks outside the house, to keep kitchen heat out during the hottest hours. Cooking indoors in hot weather is a heat exposure WHO notes for women.
records.description: Where kitchens are inside, people cook early in the morning, store food for the afternoon and cook again late in the evening. Some place open stoves in setbacks outside.
records.mechanism: Moves the heat of cooking away from the hottest hours and from living spaces.
records.benefits: Less heat indoors at midday; less exposure for whoever cooks.
records.uncertain: Food safety of food stored through hot afternoons was not examined.
records.fails_when: No outdoor space; smoke and fuel safety outside; food spoils in heat.
records.contraindications: Store cooked food safely; keep fuel and flames away from thatch.
records.equity: Shifts the timing of women's work; the study's discussion links cleaner fuels and ventilated kitchens to lower heat for women who cook.
evaluation: Measure kitchen and living-room temperature with indoor and outdoor cooking.
Food safety of food held from morning to afternoon.

records.title: Courtyards, dense lanes and shaded façades in old Rajasthan towns
records.category_basis: Described in older parts of Bikaner and in the Churu plan.

local_names.name: chowk
local_names.note: an open square or courtyard, named in the Churu plan

local_names.name: jharokha
local_names.note: an overhanging enclosed balcony, named in the Churu plan

places.place: Old walled city of Bikaner, Rajasthan

records.summary: In Bikaner's old walled city, narrow streets, internal courtyards and dense building put more of the street and walls in shade than the wide roads of the newer extension. The study describes this but reports no measurements that isolate it.
records.description: The Bikaner study compares the old walled city (narrow streets, courtyards, dense fabric) with a planned modern extension (wider roads, exposed façades) and says the older form improves passive cooling through mutual shading. The Churu plan describes courtyards, jaali, verandas and jharokhas in the same terms.
records.mechanism: Buildings shade each other and the street; courtyards can hold cooler air at night. Courtyard performance depends heavily on proportions and climate; see the solutions library record.
records.benefits: Shade without energy; social space.
records.uncertain: No measured street or indoor temperatures are reported for Bikaner; the result is described, not shown.
records.fails_when: Dense fabric can trap heat at night or limit breeze; courtyards in humid climates behave differently.
records.contraindications: Not a template for humid cities.
records.equity: Old cores are often crowded and poorly serviced; conservation can raise costs for residents.
evaluation: Measure air and radiant temperature in old and new streets on the same afternoons and nights.

records.title: Air wells in terraced houses
records.category_basis: A modern terraced house using an air well, a feature with a long history in the region's shophouses; studied as a current design, not as a tradition.
records.summary: A six-month field measurement in one single-storey terraced house in Malaysia found air-well and test-room temperatures of roughly 27.5 to 30.9 °C with humidity above 70%. The authors conclude the minimum opening rule is less effective than intended.
records.description: The house's air well (an open shaft through the house) was monitored with temperature, humidity, air-speed and WBGT instruments for six months, alongside a single-sided ventilated test room.
records.mechanism: Warm air rises and leaves through the shaft, drawing air through rooms; in humid heat, still air limits comfort.
records.benefits: No energy needed; light and air into deep plans.
records.uncertain: One house; results depend on opening size, wind and sun.
records.fails_when: Small openings; still, humid weather; noise, rain or security concerns that keep openings closed.
records.contraindications: Do not rely on it alone in dangerous heat.

requires.space: A shaft or opening through the house

records.equity: Terraced homeowners benefit; renters cannot change layouts.
evaluation: Larger openings and night ventilation compared in the same house types.

records.title: Double-height mud houses
records.category_basis: Rural houses built of local materials in Bangladesh, as the study describes.
records.summary: A field and questionnaire study of rural houses in the Dhaka region found double-height mud houses more comfortable, by measurement and by residents' responses, than single-height mud houses and corrugated iron sheet houses.
records.description: Three types of naturally ventilated rural dwellings were compared using temperature, humidity and air speed, and residents' responses.
records.mechanism: More height lets warm air rise away from occupants; earth walls change how quickly heat reaches the room.
records.benefits: Uses local materials.
records.uncertain: Sample size and dates are not in the abstract; the full paper was not reached.
records.fails_when: Flooding and damp threaten earth walls; materials are being replaced by brick and iron sheet.
records.contraindications: Structural and flood safety first.
records.equity: The abstract notes rising incomes are moving households to brick and iron sheet.
evaluation: A larger comparison with measured night-time temperatures and flood resilience.

records.title: Vernacular stilt houses
records.category_basis: Described by the study as vernacular architecture in Palu City; a house 70 to 100 years old.

local_names.name: rumah panggung
local_names.note: a common Indonesian term for raised houses; not used in the Palu abstract

records.summary: Measurements in one vernacular stilt house in Palu City recorded an outdoor peak of 36.8 °C and an indoor peak of 32 °C on the first floor, with upper rooms varying between 29.5 and 34.6 °C depending on ceiling height, roof and openings.
records.description: Indoor and outdoor temperature and humidity were logged in one house and assessed against the Indonesian comfort standard.
records.mechanism: Raising the floor lets air move underneath and keeps rooms off hot ground; roof form and openings set how hot upper rooms get.
records.benefits: Raised floors also help in floods.
records.uncertain: One house; the hottest upper rooms were close to outdoor peaks.
records.fails_when: Low ceilings or poorly ventilated upper rooms; timber decay or termites.
records.contraindications: Timber structure needs inspection and fire safety.
records.equity: Timber costs and skills limit who can build them today.
evaluation: More houses, longer periods, and night-time measurements.

records.title: Courtyard houses in Jaffna
records.category_basis: The study calls them vernacular courtyard houses.
records.summary: A conference study compared the thermal performance of two vernacular courtyard houses of different types in Jaffna and argues courtyards improve thermal performance. The abstract does not say how performance was assessed.
records.description: The study reviewed literature, identified courtyard house types in Jaffna and compared two houses in the same climate zone.
records.mechanism: Courtyards bring light and air into the house and can hold cooler air.
records.benefits: Daylight and ventilation.
records.uncertain: Method (measured or simulated) and results are not in the abstract.
records.fails_when: Courtyard proportions that let sun in at midday.
records.contraindications: None stated.

requires.space: Plot large enough for a courtyard

records.equity: Needs land many urban households lack.
evaluation: Publish measured indoor temperatures for each house type.

records.title: Earthen pots (matka) for drinking water
records.category_basis: Described as a traditional village practice in India by a livestock study and the Churu plan; observed outside most houses in Jodhpur district.
records.summary: Keeping drinking water in unglazed earthen pots, which cool it by evaporation. Researchers observed pots outside most houses in two Jodhpur villages, open to everyone; the Churu plan proposes distributing them and filling community pots in public places.
records.description: Water seeps slowly through the clay and evaporates from the outside surface, cooling the water inside. In Jodhpur district, drinking-water pots stood in front of most houses for anyone to use.
records.mechanism: Evaporative cooling through porous clay; works best in dry, moving air.
records.benefits: Cooler water without electricity; shared pots offer water to passers-by.
records.uncertain: How much cooler, and how water safety is kept, was not measured in these sources.
records.fails_when: Humid air (little evaporation); shortages; pots left uncovered or not cleaned.
records.contraindications: Water safety: covered pots, a clean dipper or tap, and regular cleaning. Cool water is not a treatment for heat illness.
records.equity: Public pots help those without water at work or on the road; depends on who refills them.

who.decides: Households, or the municipality for public pots

evaluation: Measure water temperature and microbial quality in pots in use, dry and humid seasons.

records.title: Water bottles wrapped in wet jute
records.category_basis: Observed and reported as a current practice during travel and work.
records.summary: People in Jodhpur district carry water bottles covered in a wet jute sack when travelling or working, keeping the water cooler by evaporation. The researchers observed it as near-universal; its cooling was not measured.
records.description: Carrying water bottles, sometimes covered by wet jute, was observed as a common practice during journeys and at work.
records.mechanism: Evaporation from the wet jute cools the bottle.
records.benefits: Cooler drinking water on the move.
records.uncertain: The figure caption says it can effectively keep water cool; this is the authors' description, not a measurement.
records.fails_when: Humid air; no water to re-wet.
records.contraindications: None beyond keeping the bottle clean.
records.equity: Helps workers without cool water at worksites; employers remain responsible for drinking water at work.
evaluation: Measure water temperature over a working day with and without the wrap.

records.title: Public water points: pots, taps and reservoirs
records.category_basis: Community and municipal arrangements reported in Rajasthan and West Bengal.

local_names.name: kund
local_names.note: a traditional water storage tank, named in the Churu plan

records.summary: In Jodhpur district, rural employment-scheme workers and villagers set up temporary shelters and water reservoirs; in Dalkhola, cool drinking water from public taps was a preferred way to cope, though many lacked access. The Churu plan proposes community pots and water kiosks.
records.description: Village councils and rural employment-scheme workers help set up temporary shelters, water reservoirs and huts. In West Bengal, participants named cool water from public taps as a preferred coping mechanism.
records.mechanism: Access to cool drinking water away from home.
records.benefits: Serves people working or travelling outdoors.
records.uncertain: Coverage and upkeep are not measured.
records.fails_when: Supply interruptions, unsafe water, no one responsible for refilling.
records.contraindications: Water quality checks.
records.equity: Depends on public budgets and on whose neighbourhoods get taps first.
evaluation: Map public water points against where outdoor workers are.

records.title: Summer foods and drinks: buttermilk, curd, millet and desert beans
records.category_basis: Reported seasonal food practices in Jodhpur district; described in the Churu plan.

local_names.name: ker sangri
local_names.note: a dish of desert beans and capers

records.summary: In Jodhpur district people describe eating more curd, buttermilk and millet, less fried food, and seasonal dishes such as ker sangri in summer; fruit is preferred but many say it is unaffordable. The Churu plan says such foods regulate body temperature; that is the plan's claim, not a tested effect.
records.description: Respondents preferred buttermilk, curd and dairy, ate millet flatbreads and porridge, ate fewer spicy and fried foods, and used desert beans. Some soak screw pine (kevala) flowers in pot water, believed to cool the body.
records.mechanism: Fluids such as buttermilk contribute to hydration. Claims that foods "cool" the body or regulate core temperature are cultural explanations, not tested here.
records.benefits: Familiar, local foods; fluids help hydration.
records.uncertain: No effect on body temperature or illness has been measured; ordinary drinks are not oral rehydration solution.
records.fails_when: Cost: fruit and dairy were described as unaffordable for some; food spoils in heat.
records.contraindications: Do not treat these as remedies for heat illness; seek care for symptoms.
records.equity: Affordability shaped who could adapt their diet, the study notes.
evaluation: Do hot-season diets change fluid intake or illness? Can food schemes make these foods affordable?

records.title: Reported home remedies for heat illness (documented, not recommended)
records.category_basis: Remedies described by participants as traditional.

local_names.name: multani mitti
local_names.note: bentonite clay, applied to the skin

records.summary: Villagers in Jodhpur district described applying bentonite clay to the skin, drinking or applying tamarind water, and a spice decoction for heat symptoms, alongside ORS and fluids. The study's authors note there is no scientific evidence for the decoction. These are documented here, not recommended.
records.description: Participants preferred home remedies for milder illness, including multani mitti on the body, tamarind water and paste, and a decoction of sugar candy, coriander, black pepper and cloves. They seek hospital care if a person does not recover.
records.mechanism: None established for heat illness.
records.benefits: Not established.
records.uncertain: No evidence that these prevent or treat heat illness; delaying care can be dangerous.
records.fails_when: Heat stroke and severe heat illness need urgent medical care.
records.contraindications: Not treatment guidance. For heat illness follow official health advice and seek care urgently for severe symptoms.
records.equity: Participants described understaffed health facilities and travel to the city for emergencies, which shapes reliance on home care.
evaluation: Why do people choose home care first, and what would make timely health care reachable?

records.title: Working in cooler hours
records.category_basis: Current adjustments reported by workers, supervisors and village heads.
records.summary: Shifting outdoor work to early morning and evening. In Jodhpur district, rural employment-scheme hours were moved from 9 am to 5 pm to 6 am to 11 am or noon after heat alerts; but daily-wage workers said they must keep working to eat. In Dhaka, older workers' altered schedules were largely insufficient without support.
records.description: Many participants schedule work in cooler parts of the day; supervisors halve scheme hours when a heatwave alert arrives. Labourers limit time in direct sun but cannot stop working. In Bangladesh, planning work in cooler hours was one behaviour surveyed among construction workers.
records.mechanism: Avoids the hottest hours, as WHO advises.
records.benefits: Less exposure at midday.
records.uncertain: Whether earnings, output and illness change has not been measured in these sources.
records.fails_when: Pay is by the day or piece and hours cannot be shifted; early starts clash with childcare and transport; night work brings its own risks.
records.contraindications: Shifting hours does not replace rest, shade and water during work.

requires.services: Transport at early and late hours

records.equity: Depends on employer permission and pay; the study records wage loss and sickness absence among daily-wage workers.

who.pays: Workers bear lost earnings unless protected

records.title: Regular breaks during work
records.category_basis: Reported adaptive behaviour among workers.
records.summary: Taking regular breaks was the adaptive behaviour construction workers in Bangladesh were most likely to have increased. A pilot study of informal workers in Dhaka calls for rest breaks and hydration access.
records.description: Construction workers were far more likely than welders to report increasing regular breaks (odds ratio 9.49).
records.mechanism: Rest lowers the body's heat production.
records.benefits: Lowers heat strain.
records.uncertain: Break length and pay during breaks were not reported.
records.fails_when: Breaks are unpaid or penalised.
records.contraindications: None.
records.equity: Paid breaks depend on employers and labour rules.
evaluation: Measure heat illness and earnings under paid break schedules.

records.title: Village information groups that pass on heat alerts
records.category_basis: A contemporary village arrangement described by a village council head.

local_names.name: Sajag
local_names.note: meaning alert or aware, the group's name

records.summary: A village council in Jodhpur district runs an informal group called Sajag to pass on weather updates; when the state meteorological department warns of heat, scheme hours are adjusted and residents told to drink water. Older people without smartphones may miss such messages.
records.description: Members are mainly workers, labourers and shopkeepers; messages are meant to reach everyone in the village.
records.mechanism: Turns an official warning into a local action (changed hours, reminders).
records.benefits: Fast, trusted local reach.
records.uncertain: Reach among older people and those without phones.
records.fails_when: Messages reach only phone users.
records.contraindications: None.
records.equity: Older residents believed alerts reached only smartphone owners.
evaluation: Who receives alerts, and what do they change?

records.title: Trees around homes and shared spaces
records.category_basis: Reported and observed in Rajasthan and West Bengal; trees as protection from heat are not classified as Indigenous here.
records.summary: In Dalkhola, West Bengal, trees were the primary way people coped with heat, though many noted trees being lost; in Jodhpur district, almost all households had large trees in their setbacks. At Angkor, temples with less tree cover were 1 to 5 °C warmer at night than the surrounding forest.
records.description: Participants in West Bengal preferred nature-based solutions over infrastructure; in Rajasthan, villagers valued trees, took part in planting drives and recalled the Bishnoi community's protection of trees.
records.mechanism: Shade blocks direct and reflected sun; leaves cool by evaporation.
records.benefits: Shade for people and animals; shared rest places.
records.uncertain: Cooling for people was not measured in the Indian studies; the Angkor study measures sites, not people.
records.fails_when: Water scarcity for young trees; trees cut for roads and building.
records.contraindications: Choose species suited to local water.
records.equity: Tree cover is often thinner in poorer neighbourhoods; the World Bank recommends strategic urban greening.
evaluation: Measure shade temperatures where people rest and work.

records.title: Shaded streets and covered walkways
records.category_basis: A contemporary urban arrangement, measured in Singapore; included as the measured counterpart to shaded lanes.
records.summary: On an extremely hot afternoon in Singapore, shaded spots were on average 0.8 °C cooler in air temperature and much cooler in radiant heat than paired sunlit spots, lowering heat stress categories. The World Bank lists shade and urban design as a way to cool city spaces.
records.description: Measurements at 20 pairs of sunlit and shaded sites compared air temperature, mean radiant temperature and the UTCI heat stress index.
records.mechanism: Shade mainly cuts radiant heat from the sun and hot surfaces; air temperature changes less.
records.benefits: Less heat stress for people walking, waiting and working outside.
records.uncertain: One afternoon, one district.
records.fails_when: Shade structures that trap heat or block breeze.
records.contraindications: None.
records.equity: Shade is unevenly spread across neighbourhoods.
evaluation: Map shade where outdoor workers and waiting passengers are.

records.title: Feeding infants in hot weather: water supplements and exclusive breastfeeding
records.category_basis: Giving water to young infants in hot weather is a widespread practice and advice in some settings; this record follows the evidence on it.

places.place: Low- and middle-income countries, including in Asia

records.summary: In some places relatives and health workers advise giving water to young infants in hot weather. A systematic review found no evidence that infants under six months need extra fluids in hot weather, and UNICEF advises exclusive breastfeeding for infants under six months.
records.description: The review of 18 studies found that cultural practices and advice continue to encourage water supplementation in hot seasons in some settings.
records.mechanism: Breastmilk meets young infants' fluid needs; water supplements can displace breastmilk.
records.benefits: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended even in hot conditions.
records.uncertain: Few studies; settings vary.
records.fails_when: Mothers lack water, rest or support to keep breastfeeding in heat.
records.contraindications: For a sick infant, follow health worker advice and seek care urgently for warning signs.
records.equity: Depends on mothers having water, rest and support; UNICEF advises breastfeeding mothers to drink plenty of water.
evaluation: What advice do health workers in each district give in hot weather?

records.title: Thatched sheds and water spraying for livestock
records.category_basis: Straw sheds (chappra) reported by villagers; a ventilated thatched shed tested in a dairy study.

local_names.name: chappra
local_names.note: an animal shed made of straw

places.place: Dairy research setting (India; site not stated in the abstract)

records.summary: Villagers in Jodhpur district build straw sheds (chappra) and spray water on cattle in summer. In a dairy study, cows in an open-ridge ventilated, double-slope thatched shed had a better microclimate and less heat-related drop in milk yield than cows under an asbestos roof.
records.description: Participants described straw sheds that are easy to water and keep cooler, and spraying water on animals; a controlled study compared a ventilated thatched shed with a single-slope asbestos shed.
records.mechanism: Thatch limits radiant heat from the roof; a ridge opening lets hot air escape; water on animals cools by evaporation.
records.benefits: Animal welfare and milk yield (in the dairy study).
records.uncertain: The dairy study measured animals, not the people who look after them.
records.fails_when: Water scarcity; thatch fire risk and renewal.
records.contraindications: Fire safety around thatch.
records.equity: Smallholders depend on livestock income in heat.
evaluation: Do shed designs also change heat for people working in them?

records.title: Earthen pot water for livestock
records.category_basis: The study builds on the village practice of cooling drinking water in earthen pots.
records.summary: In a chamber experiment, heat-stressed sheep given cooler earthen-pot water lost less body weight and ate more than heat-stressed sheep given water at ambient temperature.
records.description: Eighteen rams were divided into control, heat stress and heat stress with earthen pot water groups for one month.
records.mechanism: Cooler drinking water helps animals shed heat.
records.benefits: Less weight loss and better intake in heat (in sheep).
records.uncertain: A chamber, not a farm; sheep only.
records.fails_when: Water scarcity; pots not refilled.
records.contraindications: Clean water.
records.equity: Low-cost for smallholders.
evaluation: Test on farms in summer.
